name: SofaBaton X2 Universal Remote
summary: SofaBaton's flagship hub-based universal remote controls IR, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi devices with one-press activities; the closest thing to a modern Harmony Elite replacement.
verdict:
Since Logitech discontinued Harmony, SofaBaton's hub-based remotes have become the go-to replacement, and the X2 is its flagship. A **hub** sits near your equipment and translates commands into **IR, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi**, so the remote doesn't need line of sight and can control gear inside a closed cabinet. Setup runs through the SofaBaton app, and the hub links with **Alexa and Google Assistant** for voice control.

**Why Bluetooth control matters.** Some popular devices, such as Fire TV sticks and PlayStation consoles, don't respond to IR, so IR-only remotes can't control them fully. A hub that speaks Bluetooth covers those boxes too.

**Do the activity maths.** A typical movie setup is TV or projector, AV receiver, streaming box and disc player: four devices. A "Watch Movie" activity might send **six to eight commands** (power on three or four devices, switch the TV input, switch the receiver input). That's the job a hub remote does in one press, and it's what simple code-based remotes like the [GE 4-device remote](/gear/ge-universal-remote/) can't.

**Compared with the [SofaBaton X1S](/gear/sofabaton-x1s/),** the X2 is the more premium remote with a refined design; the core hub capability is similar, so if budget matters the X1S does most of the same work. The remote is rechargeable.

Owners report a learning curve when building complex activities in the app. See the [best universal remote for home theater](/best-universal-remote-for-home-theater/) roundup.
bestFor: Complex home theaters with gear in cabinets and Bluetooth devices like Fire TV or PlayStation
skipIf: You only need to control a TV and one or two IR devices

faqs.q: Can the SofaBaton X2 control a Fire TV or PS5?
faqs.a: Yes. Its hub can send Bluetooth commands, which devices like Fire TV sticks and PlayStation consoles need.

name: SofaBaton X1S Universal Remote
summary: A hub-based universal remote that handles IR, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi devices with activities and voice assistant support, for less than SofaBaton's flagship.
verdict:
The X1S brings SofaBaton's hub approach at a lower price than the [SofaBaton X2](/gear/sofabaton-x2/). The **hub** translates commands into **IR, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi**, so you can control equipment hidden in a cabinet and Bluetooth-only devices like Fire TV sticks and PlayStation consoles. It works with **Alexa and Google Assistant** via the hub, and the remote is rechargeable.

**Count your devices first.** A typical theater has a TV or projector, AV receiver, streaming box and disc player; add a motorized screen or smart lights and you're at six. Simple code-based remotes top out at four or so devices, and they can't run multi-step activities. If you have **three or more** devices that need to turn on together, a hub remote earns its price.

**Activity design tip.** Build one activity per source ("Watch Apple TV", "Play Blu-ray") rather than one big "Movie" activity. Each one then sets the right TV and [AV receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/) inputs, and switching between them only changes what's needed instead of power-cycling everything.

**IR placement.** The hub has to see your IR devices. If gear sits behind solid cabinet doors, place the hub inside the cabinet or use an IR extender.

Owners like the value and device coverage; setup through the app takes some patience. See the [best universal remote for home theater](/best-universal-remote-for-home-theater/) roundup.
bestFor: Mid-size home theaters that want hub-based control without flagship pricing
skipIf: You only control a TV and soundbar; your TV remote probably already does that

faqs.q: What's the difference between the SofaBaton X1S and X2?
faqs.a: Both use a hub to control IR, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi devices. The X2 is the more premium model, while the X1S offers most of the same core control for less.

faqs.q: Does the SofaBaton X1S need line of sight?
faqs.a: The remote talks to the hub without line of sight. The hub itself needs to see IR devices, or you can add an IR extender.

name: SofaBaton U2 Universal Remote
summary: An affordable app-programmed universal remote that controls up to 15 IR and Bluetooth devices without a hub; a sensible step up from code-based remotes.
verdict:
The SofaBaton U2 is a budget universal remote with a modern twist: you set it up through the **SofaBaton app** over Bluetooth rather than typing in codes, and it controls up to **15 devices** using **IR and Bluetooth**. There's **no hub**, so the remote itself needs line of sight to IR devices.

**Bluetooth is the key advantage.** Many budget remotes are IR-only, which rules out Bluetooth devices such as Fire TV sticks and PlayStation consoles. The U2 can pair with a Bluetooth device, so it covers more of a modern setup than the [GE universal remote](/gear/ge-universal-remote/) or the discontinued [Logitech Harmony 665](/gear/logitech-harmony-665/).

**Where the maths runs out.** Without a hub, multi-device activities rely on the remote sending commands in sequence while you point it at the gear. That works for a simple TV, receiver and streaming box setup on an open shelf. If your equipment is behind cabinet doors or you want one-press control of five or more devices, step up to the [SofaBaton X1S](/gear/sofabaton-x1s/).

**Battery and build.** It runs on replaceable batteries and is lightweight; owners describe it as good value with a few caveats about button feel and occasional app pairing hiccups.

For a second room or a small theater with gear in view, it's an easy recommendation. See the [best universal remote for home theater](/best-universal-remote-for-home-theater/) roundup.

name: Logitech Harmony 665
summary: A discontinued but still-capable activity-based IR remote for up to 10 devices; worth it only if you find one cheaply and accept that support is winding down.
verdict:
The Harmony 665 was the entry point to Logitech's activity-based remotes, controlling up to **10 devices** over **IR** with one-press activities like "Watch TV" and "Watch a Movie". Logitech **discontinued the Harmony line in 2021**, so what's on sale now is remaining stock or used units.

**What still works.** The remote is programmed with Logitech's MyHarmony desktop software, and Logitech said it would keep its servers running for existing owners, but it's no longer actively developed and new device codes aren't guaranteed. If you buy one, set it up while the software still works and save your configuration.

**Do the coverage maths.** IR-only means no control of Bluetooth devices such as Fire TV sticks and PlayStation consoles, and no control of gear in closed cabinets without line of sight. Count your devices: a TV, [AV receiver](/best-home-theater-receiver/), Apple TV and Blu-ray player all work over IR, but swap the Apple TV for a Fire TV and you'll be reaching for a second remote.

**Battery.** It runs on two AA batteries, which last a long time in an IR remote.

Owners still praise the activity buttons and ergonomics. But at similar money the [SofaBaton U2](/gear/sofabaton-u2/) adds Bluetooth and active support, and the [SofaBaton X1S](/gear/sofabaton-x1s/) adds a hub. See the [best universal remote for home theater](/best-universal-remote-for-home-theater/) roundup.

faqs.a: Logitech discontinued Harmony remotes in 2021. Existing remotes can still be configured through its software for now, but the line is no longer developed.

faqs.q: Can the Harmony 665 control a Fire TV stick?
faqs.a: No. Fire TV sticks use Bluetooth for most functions, and the Harmony 665 is IR-only.

name: GE Universal Remote 4-Device
summary: A cheap, simple code-based IR remote for up to four devices; fine for replacing a lost TV remote, but no activities, app or Bluetooth control.
verdict:
The GE 4-device universal remote is the simplest option here: an **IR** remote that you program by entering codes or running an auto-search, and it controls up to **four devices**, typically TV, cable or satellite box, streaming box and audio. It runs on **two AAA batteries**, and there's no app, hub or voice control.

**Run the device count.** A basic home theater with a TV, AV receiver, streaming box and Blu-ray player already uses all four slots. Add a projector or a second streaming device and you're out of room. And each device is controlled separately: turning on a movie setup means pressing the device button, then power, for each component, and switching inputs manually.

**IR only.** It can't control Bluetooth devices like Fire TV sticks or PlayStation consoles, and it needs line of sight. Code libraries also lag behind newer equipment, so a recent receiver or streaming box may only get basic functions.

**Where it makes sense.** As a replacement for a lost TV remote, a remote for a guest room, or a backup for grandparents who want big, simple buttons, it's ideal and nearly disposable at the price.

For a real home theater, the [SofaBaton U2](/gear/sofabaton-u2/) is the cheapest meaningful upgrade, and the [SofaBaton X1S](/gear/sofabaton-x1s/) is the best value hub remote. See the [best universal remote for home theater](/best-universal-remote-for-home-theater/) roundup.
bestFor: Replacing a lost remote or controlling a simple TV setup cheaply
skipIf: You have more than four devices or need one-press activities
pros: Simple setup with code entry or auto-search
cons: Newer devices may only get basic functions

faqs.q: How do I program a GE universal remote?
faqs.a: Enter the code for your device from GE's code list, or use the auto-search mode, which cycles through codes until your device responds.

faqs.q: Can the GE universal remote control a soundbar?
faqs.a: Often yes, if the soundbar responds to IR and has a code in GE's library. Bluetooth-only devices won't work.
